1a.html:
Smelting and matte smelting

Smelting (reduction smelting) heats an ore, usually an oxide, with a flux and a reducing agent (coke) so that the charge melts into liquid metal and an immiscible slag, with gases leaving:

\text{mineral} + \text{gangue} + \text{flux} + \text{reducing agent} \rightarrow \text{metal} + \text{slag} + \text{gas}, \qquad \mathrm{MO} + \mathrm{C} = \mathrm{M} + \mathrm{CO}

Matte smelting fuses a sulphide concentrate (usually partly roasted) with a flux, without a reducing agent, to give a matte, a molten mixture of sulphides (\mathrm{Cu_2S} and FeS), under an immiscible slag; some sulphur leaves as \mathrm{SO_2}.

BasisSmeltingMatte smelting
Chargeoxide ore, flux, cokesulphide concentrate or calcine, siliceous flux
Chemistryreduction by C and COmainly melting; Fe partly oxidised and slagged
Atmospherereducingneutral to mildly oxidising
Productcrude metal (iron, lead)matte, an intermediate that must be converted

Extraction of copper by matte smelting

The process works because copper has a greater affinity for sulphur, and iron a greater affinity for oxygen: iron is oxidised and slagged, and copper stays as \mathrm{Cu_2S}.

  1. Concentration. Chalcopyrite (\mathrm{CuFeS_2}) ore with less than 2% Cu is upgraded by froth flotation to a concentrate of about 11 to 35% Cu.
  2. Partial roasting. Part of the FeS is oxidised; the reaction is not completed, so that no higher iron oxides form:
2\,\mathrm{CuFeS_2} + \mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + 2\,\mathrm{FeS} + \mathrm{SO_2}, \qquad 2\,\mathrm{FeS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{FeO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}
  1. Matte smelting. The calcine is melted with quartz at 1200 to 1300 °C. Any copper oxide is turned back to sulphide, and FeO is slagged:
\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{FeS} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + \mathrm{FeO}, \qquad \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}

The denser matte collects below the slag; the slag is tapped off and discarded.

  1. Converting. Slag blow (air through the matte): FeS is oxidised and slagged, and the slag is poured off, leaving white metal (\mathrm{Cu_2S}):
2\,\mathrm{FeS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{FeO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}, \qquad \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}

Copper blow:

2\,\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}, \qquad 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} = 6\,\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2}

The product is blister copper, about 99% Cu.

  1. Refining. Fire refining blows air to remove the dissolved sulphur ([\mathrm{S}] + \mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{SO_2}), then removes the dissolved oxygen with hydrocarbons (poling), for example \mathrm{CH_4} + 3\,[\mathrm{O}] = \mathrm{CO} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}. The anodes are electrorefined to cathode copper of 99.99% Cu.
pts: Smelting: ore, flux and a reducing agent (coke) heated to give liquid metal, slag and gas, with a reduction such as \mathrm{MO} + \mathrm{C} = \mathrm{M} + \mathrm{CO}
Matte smelting: sulphide charge fused with flux, no reducing agent, gives a matte (molten \mathrm{Cu_2S} + FeS) and an immiscible slag
At least two contrasts: metal against an intermediate that needs converting, reducing against neutral or oxidising conditions, oxide against sulphide feed, CO against \mathrm{SO_2}
Principle: Cu has the greater affinity for S and Fe for O, so Fe goes to slag and Cu to matte (or gives the sequence concentration, roasting, smelting, converting, refining)
Concentration of chalcopyrite (below 2% Cu) by froth flotation to about 11 to 35% Cu

Partial roasting with balanced reactions (2\mathrm{CuFeS_2} + \mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + 2\mathrm{FeS} + \mathrm{SO_2}; 2\mathrm{FeS} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{FeO} + 2\mathrm{SO_2}), not taken to completion

Matte smelting with silica at 1200 to 1300 °C: \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}, and \mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{FeS} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + \mathrm{FeO} or "very little reaction, mainly melting"
Matte and slag immiscible; the denser matte settles below and the slag is removed
Converting, slag blow: 2\mathrm{FeS} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{FeO} + 2\mathrm{SO_2} and slagging with \mathrm{SiO_2}; slag poured off
Converting, copper blow: 2\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\mathrm{SO_2} and 2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} = 6\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2}, giving blister copper of about 99% Cu
Refining: fire refining (S oxidised by air, O removed by hydrocarbons or poling) and electrorefining to about 99.99% Cu
1a.watch:
• Balance the roasting reaction for FeS: 2\mathrm{FeS} + 3\mathrm{O_2}, not \mathrm{FeS} + \mathrm{O_2} (see the Correction).
  • Do not write that carbon reduces the matte: matte smelting needs no reducing agent, and copper is made from \mathrm{Cu_2S} by the reaction of \mathrm{Cu_2O} with \mathrm{Cu_2S} in the converter.
  • The roast is stopped short because \mathrm{Fe_3O_4} and \mathrm{Fe_2O_3} melt high and are hard to slag; magnetite makes the slag viscous and traps matte.
  • The slide says matte has twice the specific gravity of slag; typical values are about 5 and 3.5, so a ratio near 1.5. The point that the matte sinks is what earns the mark.

1b.html:
Given: 60 t of matte with 54% FeS, oxidised by blowing air; enough \mathrm{SiO_2} to form an \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2} slag, which is removed before the copper blow.

Find: (i) the volume of air to oxidise the FeS, (ii) the mass of slag.

Assumptions: the rest of the matte (46%) is \mathrm{Cu_2S}; 1 t = 1000 kg; air is 21% \mathrm{O_2} by volume (not printed, so stated); gas volumes at STP (0 °C, 1 atm), 22.4 \mathrm{m^3} per kmol. Molar masses: FeS 87.91, \mathrm{Cu_2S} 159.16, FeO 71.85, \mathrm{SiO_2} 60.09 kg/kmol.

Charge.

\begin{aligned} m_{\mathrm{FeS}} &= 0.54 \times 60\,000 = 32\,400\ \mathrm{kg}, \qquad m_{\mathrm{Cu_2S}} = 0.46 \times 60\,000 = 27\,600\ \mathrm{kg} \\ n_{\mathrm{FeS}} &= \frac{32\,400\ \mathrm{kg}}{87.91\ \mathrm{kg/kmol}} = 368.6\ \mathrm{kmol} \end{aligned}

The FeS is oxidised first, in the slag blow: iron has the greater affinity for oxygen, so any \mathrm{Cu_2O} formed is turned back to \mathrm{Cu_2S} by FeS until the iron is slagged.

(i) Air for the FeS

2\,\mathrm{FeS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{FeO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}
\begin{aligned} n_{\mathrm{O_2}} &= \tfrac{3}{2}\,n_{\mathrm{FeS}} = 1.5 \times 368.6 = 552.8\ \mathrm{kmol} \\ V_{\mathrm{O_2}} &= 552.8 \times 22.4 = 12\,380\ \mathrm{m^3} \\ V_{\text{air}} &= \frac{V_{\mathrm{O_2}}}{0.21} = 4.762 \times 12\,380 = 58\,970\ \mathrm{m^3} \end{aligned}

Answer: about 5.90\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m^3} of air at STP.

(ii) Slag

Each kmol of FeS gives 1 kmol of FeO, which takes up 1 kmol of \mathrm{SiO_2}:

\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}\qquad (71.85 + 60.09 = 131.94\ \mathrm{kg/kmol})
\begin{aligned} m_{\mathrm{FeO}} &= 368.6 \times 71.85 = 26\,480\ \mathrm{kg} \\ m_{\mathrm{SiO_2}} &= 368.6 \times 60.09 = 22\,150\ \mathrm{kg} \\ m_{\text{slag}} &= 26\,480 + 22\,150 = 48\,630\ \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}

Answer: about 48.6 t of \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2} slag (the course's rounded masses, 32\,400 \times \tfrac{144}{176} \times \tfrac{132}{72}, give 48,600 kg).
pts: (i) Splits the charge into 32,400 kg FeS and 27,600 kg \mathrm{Cu_2S}, and states the air composition used (21% \mathrm{O_2}) and STP
(i) Balanced reaction 2\mathrm{FeS} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{FeO} + 2\mathrm{SO_2}
(i) FeS = 32\,400/87.9 = 368.6 kmol (or works directly in kg: 176 kg FeS needs 3 \times 22.4\ \mathrm{m^3} \mathrm{O_2})
(i) \mathrm{O_2} needed 552.8 kmol, about 12,380 \mathrm{m^3} at STP (12,370 with rounded masses)
(i) Air = V_{\mathrm{O_2}}/0.21 \approx 5.90\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m^3} (58,900 to 59,000 \mathrm{m^3}; about 59,250 with 20.9% \mathrm{O_2})
(ii) FeO formed from the FeS, 1 kmol per kmol: about 26,480 kg (26,500 with rounded masses)
(ii) Slag reaction \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}, molar mass 131.9 (132) kg/kmol
(ii) \mathrm{SiO_2} taken up about 22,150 kg, or slag = (131.9/71.85) \times FeO
(ii) Slag about 48.6 t (4.86\times10^{4} kg)
1b.watch:
• The paper prints no part marks; the points split them 10 + 10 between (i) and (ii).
  • This version does not print the air composition: say that you take air as 21% \mathrm{O_2} (79% \mathrm{N_2}) by volume, so 4.76 \mathrm{m^3} of air per \mathrm{m^3} of \mathrm{O_2}.
  • Read "60 tons" as metric tonnes, as the course solution does. In short tons (907.2 kg) every answer is 0.907 times smaller.
  • Do not add the \mathrm{Cu_2S} to the slag or its oxygen to part (i): the question asks only for the air that oxidises the FeS.
  • Extra depth: the copper blow (\mathrm{Cu_2S} + \mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2} overall) needs another 173.4 kmol \mathrm{O_2}, about 18,500 \mathrm{m^3} of air, and gives about 22.0 t of blister copper.

2a.html:
Essential features of a successful hydrometallurgical process

  1. Selective, fast leaching. A cheap reagent must dissolve the value mineral (or, in some cases, the gangue) selectively and at a useful rate, without being wasted on the gangue.
  2. Suitable preparation. Grinding, concentration or roasting must expose the mineral or make it soluble and porous.
  3. Clean separation. The leach liquor must separate readily from the residue by settling, thickening and filtration, with washing so little dissolved metal is lost with the tailings.
  4. Recovery of the metal from the liquor in the required form and purity, by purification and then precipitation, cementation, electrolysis, solvent extraction or ion exchange.
  5. Regeneration of the reagent, purified, readjusted and recycled (acid is regenerated during electrowinning).
  6. Plant and effluents. Materials of construction must resist corrosion, and effluents must be disposed of safely.

When it is preferred to a pyrometallurgical process

  1. Lean ores. Smelting would heat and slag all the gangue, but most leaching reagents hardly attack siliceous gangue, so cost follows the metal content: gold at about 10 g/t is cyanided at a profit.
  2. Complex ores. Selective, controlled steps recover valuable by-products.
  3. Sulphide ores where SO2 is a problem. Leaching keeps the sulphur in solution.
  4. Costly coke, the fuel and reductant of smelting.
  5. Small or growing output. A leach plant can start small and expand; a smelter must be large to pay.
  6. Pure compounds, metal powders or reactive metals, which are hard to refine by fire.

For rich ores and concentrates, pyrometallurgy usually needs less energy per tonne of metal.
pts: Selective and reasonably fast dissolution of the value mineral by a cheap reagent, with little loss to the gangue
Suitable ore preparation (grinding, concentration, roasting)
Easy separation of the liquor from the residue, with washing to limit soluble losses
Recovery of the metal from the liquor in the required purity, naming methods (precipitation, cementation, electrolysis, solvent extraction, ion exchange)
Regeneration and recycling of the reagent
Corrosion-resistant plant and safe effluent disposal
Preferred for low-grade ores, since the gangue is not heated or slagged (for example gold at about 10 g/t)
Preferred for complex ores, with by-product recovery
Preferred for sulphide ores, avoiding SO2
Two further conditions: costly coke, small plant that can expand, pure compounds or reactive metals, or rich ores left to pyrometallurgy

• The slides do not list "essential features" as such; build them from the four steps and the reagent criteria, and phrase each as a requirement the process must meet. A student who gives the four steps (leaching, liquor separation, metal recovery, reagent recovery) as the features earns the step points above; advantages written under this heading earn the condition points instead.
  • Do not claim hydrometallurgy always uses less energy: for rich ores the book says pyrometallurgy usually needs less per tonne of metal.

2b.fix: • Slide 65 (and the course book p 28) writes the elution step as \mathrm{R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 4Cl \rightarrow 4RCl + UO_2(SO_4)}. Sulphur (3 against 1) and charge do not balance, and chloride must be \mathrm{Cl^-}. The uranium returns to solution as \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}, or equivalently \mathrm{UO_2SO_4 + 2SO_4^{2-}}, as written in the Answer. The book's loading equation also prints \mathrm{2SO_3^{-4}} for \mathrm{2SO_4^{2-}}.
2b.html:
Why the leach liquor is purified

Leaching is rarely completely selective, so the pregnant liquor also carries ions that interfere with later steps or would leave unacceptable impurity levels in the product. Purification lowers their concentration, or removes the desired metal selectively and leaves the impurities behind. The common methods are selective precipitation, ion exchange and solvent extraction.

Principle

Metal ions in solution exchange with specific ions held by a solid (a resin) or by a second liquid phase. The exchange is reversible and stoichiometric, so it can (i) remove unwanted ions from the solution and (ii) concentrate a selected metal ion.

The resin is an insoluble, chemically stable, rigid 3-D polymer framework, made as small hard porous beads (0.5-1 mm) of high surface area. Functional groups bonded to the framework supply the exchangeable ions: the framework fixes the physical properties, the functional groups control the selectivity.

\begin{aligned} \text{cation exchanger:}&\quad \mathrm{2\,R{-}SO_3H + Cu^{2+} \rightleftharpoons (R{-}SO_3)_2Cu + 2H^+}\\ \text{anion exchanger:}&\quad \mathrm{R^+Cl^- + A^- \rightleftharpoons R^+A^- + Cl^-} \end{aligned}

The cycle

  1. Loading (sorption): clear pregnant liquor flows through columns of resin; the resin takes up the metal ion and releases its own ion. The barren solution is dumped.
  2. Elution (stripping): a relatively small volume of strong solution reverses the reaction, giving a concentrated, pure eluate.
  3. Regeneration: the resin is returned to its original form, ready for sorption again.

Example: uranium from sulphuric acid leach liquor

Uranium forms the complex anion \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}, while the impurity metals are mostly cations, so an anion-exchange resin takes up the uranium and leaves the impurities in solution. Low-grade ores (about 0.2 % \mathrm{U_3O_8}) are treated this way.

\begin{aligned} \text{loading:}&\quad \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-} + 2R_2SO_4 \rightarrow R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 2SO_4^{2-}}\\ \text{elution (acidified chloride):}&\quad \mathrm{R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 4Cl^- \rightarrow 4RCl + [UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}\\ \text{regeneration:}&\quad \mathrm{4RCl + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2R_2SO_4 + 4HCl} \end{aligned}

Plant practice (resin-in-column)

Columns A and B load in series while C is eluted. When A is saturated it goes to elution, B leads and the freshly eluted C becomes the tail; the change-overs repeat endlessly. The flow is counter-current: fresh liquor meets nearly loaded resin, and fresh resin meets nearly exhausted liquor.

Why it purifies and concentrates

Ions the resin does not take stay in the barren solution (purification). Loading and elution are almost 100 % efficient, so the concentration factor is about V_{\text{liquor}}/V_{\text{eluate}} (concentration). The exchange depends on the size and valence of the ions, their concentration, the nature of the resin and the temperature.
pts: Need for purification: leaching is not selective, impurities interfere or contaminate the product; ion exchange is one of the methods (with selective precipitation and solvent extraction)
Principle: ions in solution exchange with ions held on a solid resin (or a second liquid); reversible and stoichiometric; removes unwanted ions or concentrates a selected one
Resin: insoluble, chemically stable 3-D polymer framework as porous beads (about 0.5-1 mm); bonded functional groups supply the exchangeable ions and control selectivity
A general exchange reaction for a cation or an anion exchanger, for example \mathrm{2R{-}SO_3H + Cu^{2+} \rightleftharpoons (R{-}SO_3)_2Cu + 2H^+}
The cycle: loading in columns, elution with a small volume of strong solution to give a concentrated eluate, regeneration of the resin
Uranium is the complex anion \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}} while impurities are cations, so an anion resin is selective
Uranium reactions for loading, elution with chloride and regeneration (1 each; elution balanced with the uranyl sulphate complex, or \mathrm{UO_2SO_4 + 2SO_4^{2-}})
Plant: resin in tall columns, A and B loading in series while C is eluted, then change-over; counter-current contact
Purification (impurity ions stay in the barren solution) and concentration (eluate volume much smaller, nearly 100 % efficient steps)
Factors: ion size and valence, concentration, nature of the resin, temperature

• The same question was set in 2014-15 (3b) and 2020-21 (7a); the answer is the same.
  • No sketch is asked, so none is credited; the column figure only shows the change-over.
  • In the uranium equations \mathrm{R^+} is the fixed quaternary ammonium group of the anion resin, so \mathrm{R_2SO_4} is the resin in its sulphate form and RCl in its chloride form.
  • Uranium is taken by an anion resin because it is in the anion; a cation resin would load the impurity metals instead.

3a.html:
Percolation (vat, or sand) leaching is the leaching of a bed of crushed low-grade ore held in large tanks, through which the leach solution percolates.

Ore preparation. The ore is crushed to about 5-20 mm, coarse enough for the solvent to pass freely through the voids. Fines and clay are screened out because they block the bed and lower its permeability; clayey ores do not suit this method.

Operation of one vat. The ore is loaded into the vat and the vat is filled with leach solution (for example dilute \mathrm{H_2SO_4} for an oxidised copper ore). After the solution has been in contact with the ore for a set time it is drained off and fresh solution is added.

Counter-current series. Leaching is carried out in a row of vats at once, the solution from one vat cycling to the next (sketch):

  1. The fresh, strongest solution enters the vat whose ore has been leached longest.
  2. It then passes to vats with progressively newer ore, so the first leach of a fresh charge is made with weak (spent) solution.
  3. The pregnant liquor leaves from the vat holding the newest ore and goes to metal recovery.
  4. At each step one vat is being loaded with fresh ore and one is being emptied, and every role moves one vat along (step 1 to step 2).

So the particles that are hardest to dissolve meet the strongest solution, while fresh ore is still readily attacked by the weak solution, and the reagent is used up before the liquor leaves.

Recovery and discharge. With 10 or more leach cycles, 80-90% of the metal values are recovered. The leached ore is then washed with water one or more times, to recover the entrained solution, and the tailings are dug out.

Assessment. It is essentially a batch process: a vat must be charged and emptied while it is out of operation. Even so, it is the most efficient method known for treating large tonnages of low-grade ore.
pts: Sketch: a row of vats with ore beds, solution piped from the bottom of one vat to the top of the next
Sketch labels: fresh solution into the most-leached vat, pregnant liquor out of the newest-ore vat, one vat loading and one unloading
Sketch or text shows that the roles move one vat along at each step
Ore crushed to about 5-20 mm, coarse enough for free percolation; fines and clay removed to keep the bed permeable
Vat filled with solution, held for a contact time, then drained and refilled with fresh solution
Counter-current principle: the strongest solution meets the longest-leached ore and the newest ore is first leached with weak (spent) solution
Reason: the hardest-to-dissolve particles meet the strongest solution while fresh ore is still attacked by weak solution
10 or more leach cycles recover about 80-90% of the metal values
At the end the ore is washed with water and the leached ore (tailings) removed
Batch process (vat out of use while charged and emptied) but the most efficient method for large tonnages of low-grade ore

  • "Fresh (strong) solution in" at the vat with the oldest ore; "pregnant solution out" at the vat with the newest ore.
  • One vat labelled "loading fresh ore" and one "unloading leached ore".

3a.watch:
• "First leach weak, final leach strongest" refers to a given charge of ore; do not write that fresh solution is fed to fresh ore.
  • Percolation needs a permeable bed: fine ground slimes go to agitation leaching instead.
  • Heap and dump leaching also rely on percolation, but on piles of ore on an impervious base, not in tanks; this question is about vat leaching.

3b.html:
An impurity behaves according to its electrode potential relative to the metal being treated and to whether it forms soluble ions. Copper electrorefining is the standard example.

In electrorefining (impurities in the anode)

  1. Nobler than the metal (Au, Ag, Pt metals in Cu; E^\circ well above +0.34 V): they do not dissolve and fall as anode slime and are recovered. A little chloride precipitates any dissolved Ag as AgCl.
  2. Less noble (Ni -0.25, Fe -0.44, Zn -0.76 V): they dissolve with the copper and accumulate in the electrolyte but do not deposit (far more negative potentials). As they build up they replace \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} and raise the resistance, so part of the electrolyte is bled (Ni recovered as \mathrm{NiSO_4}).
  3. Close to the metal (As, Sb, Bi, standard potentials about +0.2 to +0.3 V): they partly dissolve and partly go to slime. They may co-deposit or form fine "floating slime" that is occluded in the cathode, so they are the most harmful. They are controlled by bleeding, liberator cells and keeping enough As to precipitate Sb and Bi.
  4. Insoluble compounds: selenides and tellurides (\mathrm{Cu_2Se}, \mathrm{Ag_2Se}, \mathrm{Cu_2Te}) go to slime; Pb forms insoluble \mathrm{PbSO_4}; Sn forms an insoluble basic salt. \mathrm{Cu_2O} dissolves chemically, \mathrm{Cu_2O + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + Cu + H_2O}, enriching the electrolyte in copper.

In electrowinning (impurities in the electrolyte)

  1. Nobler ions (Cu, Cd, Co in zinc electrolyte) co-deposit, so the solution is purified first (zinc-dust cementation).
  2. Ions that lower the hydrogen overvoltage (Co, Ni, Sb, Ge) start hydrogen evolution and re-dissolve the zinc deposit; the current efficiency can collapse.
  3. Redox ions (\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}, \mathrm{MnO_4^-/Mn^{2+}}) are reduced at the cathode and re-oxidised at the anode, wasting current. Chloride can evolve \mathrm{Cl_2} and corrode lead anodes.

Conclusion: noble impurities report to slime, base ones to the electrolyte, and those near the metal's potential, or those that lower hydrogen overvoltage, threaten cathode purity and efficiency.
pts: Classifies impurities by electrode potential relative to the metal being refined or won
Nobler impurities (Au, Ag, Pt metals) do not dissolve and report to the anode slime (Ag fixed as AgCl by chloride)
Less noble impurities (Ni, Fe, Zn) dissolve and accumulate in the electrolyte without depositing; they lower the \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} content, so the electrolyte is bled and purified
Impurities close in potential (As, Sb, Bi) partly dissolve, may co-deposit or form floating slime; controlled by bleeding, liberator cells
Insoluble compounds: selenides, tellurides, \mathrm{PbSO_4}, tin salts go to slime; \mathrm{Cu_2O} dissolves chemically and enriches the electrolyte
Electrowinning: nobler ions co-deposit, so the leach liquor is purified first (e.g. cementation)
Electrowinning: impurities that lower hydrogen overvoltage (Co, Ni, Sb, Ge) or redox ions (\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}) lower the current efficiency
Concludes which group threatens cathode purity and which threatens efficiency
3b.watch:
• The course slides for this topic were not available; this answer follows the standard textbook treatment, so check it against the lecture notes.
  • Build the answer on the potential order (noble, base, close to the metal); a bare list of impurities earns little.
  • The same question was set in 2015-16 Q4b and (10 marks) 2014-15 Q4c.
  • "Discuss" also wants the consequences (cathode purity, current efficiency, electrolyte control), not only where each impurity goes.

4a.html:
Relative activity. The electrochemical series ranks metals by their standard reduction potential against the hydrogen electrode (0 V). The more negative E^\circ, the more reactive the metal and the harder its ion is to reduce: Au +1.50, Ag +0.80, Cu +0.34, H 0.00, Ni -0.25, Fe -0.44, Zn -0.76, Mn -1.18, Al -1.66, Mg -2.37, Na -2.71 V.

Cathode competition. In water the metal ion competes with hydrogen, and the reaction with the more positive deposition potential wins:

E_{\mathrm{M}} = E^\circ_{\mathrm{M}} + \frac{0.0592}{z}\log a_{\mathrm{M^{z+}}} - \eta_{\mathrm{M}}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{H}} = -0.0592\,\mathrm{pH} - \eta_{\mathrm{H}}

The metal deposits when E_{\mathrm{M}} > E_{\mathrm{H}}; \eta_{\mathrm{H}} is the hydrogen overvoltage on the cathode surface.

1. Metals nobler than hydrogen (Cu, Ag, Au). E_{\mathrm{M}} > E_{\mathrm{H}} even in strong acid and at low metal activity, so they deposit readily. Hydrogen appears mainly when the current density approaches the limiting current. Copper is won from about 150-180 g/L \mathrm{H_2SO_4} at 85-95 % current efficiency.

2. Less noble metals with a high hydrogen overvoltage (Zn, Cd, Pb, Sn, Mn). By equilibrium hydrogen should evolve first, but on these metals \eta_{\mathrm{H}} is about 0.7-1 V (against below 0.1 V on Pt), which pushes E_{\mathrm{H}} below E_{\mathrm{M}}. Zinc is won at 400-600 A/m^2, 35-40 ^\circC, on Al cathodes, at about 90 % efficiency, but only from a deeply purified electrolyte: Co, Ni, Sb, Ge lower \eta_{\mathrm{H}} and re-dissolve the zinc.

3. Less noble metals with a low hydrogen overvoltage (Fe, Ni, Co). They need a weakly acid (pH about 2-4), warm electrolyte and give lower efficiency.

4. Very reactive metals (Al, Mg, Na, Ca, Li, Ti). E^\circ lies below about -1.6 V: no attainable overvoltage stops hydrogen evolution, the current goes to \mathrm{H_2}, and any metal formed reacts with water:

\mathrm{2Al + 6H_2O \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3 + 3H_2}

Conclusion. Whether a metal can be electrowon from water is set by its potential relative to hydrogen, corrected for overvoltage, pH and concentration. The most reactive metals are won by fused-salt electrolysis: Al from cryolite-alumina, Mg from \mathrm{MgCl_2}, Na from NaCl.
pts: Explains the electrochemical series: metals ranked by E^\circ against hydrogen (0 V), more negative means more reactive, with values
At the cathode the reaction with the more positive deposition potential occurs first; metal ion and \mathrm{H^+} compete (Nernst forms for both)
Nobler metals (Cu, Ag, Au) deposit readily even from strong acid; hydrogen mainly near the limiting current
Less noble metals: thermodynamically hydrogen should be discharged first
Hydrogen overvoltage (high on Zn, Pb, Hg; low on Pt) moves the hydrogen potential below that of the metal, so Zn, Cd, Pb, Mn can deposit
Operating conditions for zinc (high current density, low temperature, pure electrolyte free of Co, Ni, Sb, Ge) and about 90 % efficiency
Fe, Ni, Co with low overvoltage need pH control and give lower efficiency
Very reactive metals (Al, Mg, Na; E^\circ below about -1.6 V): hydrogen evolves instead and the metal would react with water (balanced equation)
Concludes that such metals are won by fused-salt electrolysis, with examples (Hall-Heroult Al, Mg from \mathrm{MgCl_2}, Na from NaCl)
States the overall criterion: potential relative to hydrogen, corrected for overvoltage, pH and concentration

• The course slides for this topic were not available; this answer follows the standard textbook treatment, so check it against the lecture notes.
  • A list of the series alone earns little; the marks are for the hydrogen competition and the overvoltage argument.
  • Overvoltage values change with current density, temperature and surface; quote them as "about" and give the trend.

  • Mercury cathodes discharge even Na, as an amalgam (chlor-alkali cells); this is a special case, not a way to win the solid metal.

5a.html:
Recycling as a source of metals

Metals from ores are primary metals; metals from scrap are secondary metals. Recycling has become a major source because:

  1. Scrap is already metallic. It needs only refining, at best only melting; mining, ore dressing and the reduction of the oxide or sulphide (breaking metal-oxygen or metal-sulphur bonds) are all skipped.
  2. Energy and CO2 savings: energy saved is about 95% for Al, 85% for Cu and 60-75% for steel; CO2 falls by about 90%, 65% and 50%. Primary metallurgy gives about 7-9% of world CO2.
  3. Fewer, simpler operations: less pollution, no mine or tailings, less water, and cheaper metal.
  4. Conservation of resources: high-grade ore is limited; copper ores fell from about 4% Cu a century ago to 1% or less, and leaner ore costs more energy.
  5. Demand and security: metal demand may double by 2050; urban mining supplies Cu, Au and critical metals (Li, Co, rare earths).
  6. Equal quality: no test distinguishes secondary from primary metal; some of the best stainless steels are made wholly from scrap. In Bangladesh about 75% of steelmaking scrap (about 1.5 Mt in 2005) was ship scrap.

Classification of scrap by availability

  1. Home scrap: generated during primary or secondary metal production in the plant, such as defective castings and sheet edge trimmings. Known composition, no collection or sorting; always recycled at once.
  2. Prompt industrial scrap: generated while manufacturing metal articles, such as turnings and stamping offcuts (machined parts can yield up to 50% scrap). Clean, returned quickly; its amount follows manufacturing activity.
  3. Obsolete scrap: products no longer useful, such as old rails, machinery, cars and ships. Supply depends on product lifetime (car 10-12 years, lead-acid battery 2-4 years) and scrap price; it must be collected and sorted, and it offers the most room for more recycling.
pts: Scrap is already metallic, so only melting and refining are needed and the reduction (bond-breaking) step is saved
Energy savings with numbers: about 95% Al, 85% Cu, 60-75% steel
Fewer operations, less CO2 and pollution (CO2 cut 90% Al, 65% Cu, 50% steel, or primary metal 7-9% of world CO2), no mine or tailings
Conservation of limited high-grade ore: Cu grade from about 4% to 1% or less
Rising demand and urban mining of critical metals, or equal quality of secondary metal (stainless from scrap, ship scrap in Bangladesh)
Home scrap: defined as scrap from metal production, with an example, always recycled in the plant
Prompt industrial scrap: defined as scrap from manufacturing articles, with an example (turnings, offcuts, up to 50% from machining)
Obsolete scrap: end-of-life products with examples; depends on product lifetime and price; needs collection and sorting

  • Do not swap home and prompt scrap: home scrap comes from the metal producer, prompt scrap from the manufacturer that uses the metal.
  • Home and prompt scrap are recycled whatever the scrap price; obsolete scrap is price-sensitive.

5b.fix: Slide 6 of the introduction deck (and Table 1.3 of the book reading) gives zinc in the Pacific nodules as 0.46 wt% with a reserve of 0.7 billion tonnes. The two do not agree: 0.46% of 1.5 trillion tonnes of nodules is 6.9 billion tonnes. The tonnage of 0.7 billion tonnes corresponds to about 0.047 wt% Zn, the usual average for Pacific nodules, so the weight percent should read about 0.05%. The other rows are consistent; for example 0.2386 \times 1.5\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{t} = 358\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{t} of Mn.
5b.html:
After the earth's crust, the oceans are the second source of metals.

  1. Sea water covers nearly 70% of the earth's surface and holds about 3.5% dissolved solids with about 70 elements, at nearly uniform composition. Na (10,500 g per tonne) and Mg (1270 g per tonne) are abundant: a cubic kilometre holds about 1.3 million tonnes of Mg, and Mg and salt are produced commercially from it. Cu, Zn and Au (0.000005 g per tonne) are too dilute to recover.
  2. Manganese nodules: about 1.5 trillion tonnes lie on the Pacific floor, averaging 24% Mn and 14% Fe with Ni, Cu and Co. They hold about 358 billion tonnes of Mn, 14.7 billion of Ni and 5.2 billion of Co, far above land reserves, and are renewable (about 10 million tonnes form each year) while land deposits are depleted.

Limit: they lie at about 5000 m, so collection is costly and environmentally sensitive; they are a vast future reserve of Mn, Ni, Co and Cu.
pts: Sea water covers about 70% of the surface, holds about 3.5% dissolved solids and about 70 elements: a huge, uniform dilute solution
Gives abundant elements (Na 10,500, Mg 1270 g per tonne) and states that Mg has been produced commercially from sea water
Notes that trace metals such as Cu, Zn and Au are too dilute to recover economically
Manganese nodules: about 1.5 trillion tonnes on the Pacific floor, about 24% Mn and 14% Fe with Ni, Cu, Co; reserves such as 358 billion tonnes Mn, far above land reserves
Nodules are renewable (about 10 million tonnes form a year) whereas land deposits are depleted
Limitation: depth of about 5000 m, costly collection and environmental concern, so mainly a future source

• "Explain" needs both sources, sea water and sea-bed nodules, with numbers; a list of elements alone is thin.

Industrially, \mathrm{Mg(OH)_2} is precipitated from sea water with lime, converted to \mathrm{MgCl_2} and electrolysed as a fused salt.
  • Do not quote the book's remark that only nodules shallower than about 300 m can be mined; pilot collectors have already lifted nodules from about 4 to 5 km depth, though commercial mining is still being developed.

5c.html:
Commercial size reduction applies stress in three ways, and each gives a characteristic fragment size.

  1. Slow compression. Stress builds up gradually throughout the particle until the resolved tensile and shear stresses are just enough to propagate the pre-existing cracks. The largest cracks run first and relieve the stress, so fracture occurs at only a few places. Product: a few relatively large pieces, close to the original size, with few fines. Examples: jaw, gyratory and smooth roll crushers; rods rolling over one another in a rod mill.
  1. Fast compression (impact). Stress is applied so quickly that it rises far above the level needed for the largest crack: existing cracks are extended and new cracks are formed, so the particle shatters. Product: fragments much smaller than the original, with a broad size distribution. Examples: hammer and stamp mills, and the impact zone (toe) of a ball mill.
  1. Abrasion. Rubbing against neighbouring particles or hard surfaces generates high shear stresses only near the particle surface, so fracture is localised there. Product: a bimodal distribution, one peak close to the original size (the worn core) and the other at very small sizes (the fines rubbed off). Examples: zones A and B of a ball mill, attrition grinding.

Relation. The more rapidly and locally the stress is applied, the finer the fragments: slow compression gives coarse products, impact fine ones, and abrasion fines plus an almost unbroken core. Strain rate, particle size and shape, and microstructure (pre-existing cracks) also change the strength, so the distribution is predicted only empirically.
pts: Names the three techniques: slow compression, fast compression (impact) and abrasion
Slow compression: stress rises until the largest pre-existing cracks propagate, fracture at few places
Slow compression gives a few relatively large pieces close to the original size, with an example machine
Fast compression: existing cracks extended and new cracks formed
Fast compression gives fragments much smaller than the original, with an example
Abrasion: high shear stresses at the surface, fracture localised there
Abrasion gives a bimodal distribution: one peak near the original size and one at very small sizes
Sketch or statement relating the size distributions, or the factors (strain rate, size, shape, microstructure) that make the result variable

  • The bimodal product of abrasion is the point most often missed: the core is barely reduced while the fines are very small.
  • Same question as 2017-18 Q5(d) and 2011-12 Q1(c).

6a.html:
Both are primary crushers that nip lumps in a chamber narrowing downward. A gyratory crusher is a jaw crusher with circular jaws, between which material is being crushed at some point at all times.

Motionswing jaw reciprocates about a top pivothead on a spindle hung at the top gyrates (eccentric at the bottom)
Actionintermittent: crushes on the closing stroke onlycontinuous: one side crushes while the other discharges
Loaduneven, needs flywheelsuniform power draft, less maintenance
Speed250 to 400 strokes/min125 to 425 gyrations/min
Size quoted asgape × width, e.g. 66 × 84 inmouth opening, e.g. 12 in
Capacitylowermuch greater for the same feed, up to about 4500 t/h
Clayey orehandles it bettermore likely to clog

The gyratory also has a shorter throw and stops flat slabs. Reduction ratio and power per tonne are about the same, so the jaw crusher suits small plants and the gyratory large tonnages.

Motion: the swing jaw reciprocates about a pivot at the top, while the head gyrates on a spindle hung at the top, driven by a bottom eccentric
Crushing is intermittent (closing stroke only) in the jaw crusher but continuous in the gyratory, with crushing and discharge going on at once
The jaw crusher has an uneven load needing flywheels; the gyratory has a nearly uniform power draft and less maintenance
The gyratory has a much larger capacity for the same feed size (up to about 4500 t/h); the jaw crusher suits small installations
One further difference: how the size is quoted, speeds (250 to 400 strokes against 125 to 425 gyrations per min), shorter throw, clogging with clayey ore, or flat slabs

  • Gyratory crusher: fixed concave, conical head on a spindle hung at the top, the gap closing on one side and opening on the other.

  • The reduction ratio is about the same for both; do not claim the gyratory gives a larger one.
  • In industry a gyratory is often quoted as gape × mantle diameter (for example 54 × 74 in); the course book quotes the mouth opening only.

6b.html:
A ball mill is a horizontal cylinder, 30 to 50% filled with hard steel or ceramic balls and the ore (usually with water), rotating about its axis. The balls are free to move, and the size reduction comes from the motion of this charge.

Lifting. As the shell rotates, friction and the liner lift the charge up the rising side. At the shoulder, centrifugal action no longer balances the weight. The charge then falls under gravity, rolling down the surface (cascading) or thrown clear in free flight (cataracting), and lands at the toe.

Zones (see sketch).

  1. Zone A (against the rising shell): most of the charge is lifted with the lining, but some moves in the opposite direction (shearing). Size reduction by abrasion and impact.
  2. Zone B (the sloping surface): particles move with their neighbours, in intimate contact, tumbling over each other. Abrasion and impact; this is the major grinding zone.
  3. Free fall: no contact between particles, so no size reduction until they land.
  4. Zone C, the impact zone (toe): size reduction solely by impact of particles that fell from the opposite side. The fall must land on the charge, not on the bare liner, or liner wear rises sharply.

Speed. The critical speed holds a particle on the shell for a full turn, Mg = 2Mv^2/D with v = \pi D N/60:

N_c = \frac{42.3}{\sqrt{D}}\ \mathrm{rpm}\quad (D\ \text{in m})

Too slow, the balls only roll down (cascading) and grinding is limited; too fast, the charge sticks to the shell (centrifuging) and there is hardly any grinding. Mills run at 65 to 82% of N_c: for D = 2 m, N_c = 29.9 rpm and the mill runs at about 19 to 25 rpm.

Liners and filling. Profiled (lifter) liners lift the charge higher at a given speed; they reduce shearing but increase the action in zone B. The filling (30 to 50%) sets the share of the charge in each zone, so it controls the breakage mechanism and the grinding rate.
pts: Neat sketch: shell with direction of rotation, charge lifted to the shoulder, free-fall paths onto the toe, zones A, B and C and the no-grinding region labelled
Charge lifted up the rising side by the lining until, at the shoulder, centrifugal action no longer balances the weight and it falls under gravity
Zone A: most of the charge lifted with the lining, some opposite movement (shearing); size reduction by abrasion and impact
Zone B: particles in intimate contact tumbling over each other; abrasion and impact; the major grinding zone
Free fall: no contact between particles, so no size reduction until the impact zone
Zone C (toe): size reduction solely by impact; falling charge should strike the charge, not the liner, to limit liner wear
Critical speed N_c = 42.3/\sqrt{D} rpm; too slow gives cascading (little grinding), too fast gives centrifuging (no grinding); runs at 65 to 82% of N_c
Profiled (lifter) liners raise the lift at a given speed, reduce shearing and increase action in zone B
Filling of 30 to 50% sets the proportion of charge in each zone, hence the breakage mechanism and rate

6c.fix: • Slide 36 says a 100-mesh product has passed a screen with 100 openings per square inch. Mesh number is the number of openings per linear inch, so a 100-mesh screen has 100 openings per inch (10 000 per square inch) and an aperture of about 0.15 mm.
6c.html:
Closed circuit grinding is running a mill (usually a ball mill) with a classifier or screen that splits the discharge into the finished product and the oversize, which returns to the mill as the circulating load (commonly 200 to 1000% of the new feed).

Why. A ball mill also grinds particles already fine enough, so batch grinding to, say, all minus 65 mesh over-grinds much of the ore (hard to concentrate, energy wasted), while a short open-circuit pass leaves oversize. In closed circuit the ore passes quickly with little over-grinding (sliming), and the classifier keeps the oversize in the circuit.
pts: Defines it: the mill works with a classifier or screen that takes the discharge and returns the oversize to the mill
Names the returned stream the circulating load (about 200 to 1000% of the new feed)
Reason: batch or long grinding over-grinds (sliming, energy waste), and open circuit leaves oversize
Result: rapid passage through the mill with little over-grinding and a product of the required size
6c.src: Size reduction, slides 36-40; Size reduction reading (book Ch 2), pp 16-17
6c.watch:
• Rod mills give a narrow size range with few fines and are usually run in open circuit; ball mills are the ones closed with a classifier.
  • Mesh number counts openings per linear inch: 65 mesh has 65 openings per inch, an aperture of about 0.21 mm.

7a.html:
Recovery is the percentage of the total metal in the ore (feed) that is recovered in the concentrate; 90% recovery means 10% of the metal is lost in the tailing.

Ratio of concentration is the weight of feed treated per unit weight of concentrate: 1 t of concentrate from 20 t of ore is 20 to 1.

The two are independent, so both are needed: picking a few lumps of pure galena gives a high ratio but very low recovery.

Derivation (two-product formula). Feed F of assay f gives concentrate C, c and tailing T, t. By definition R = Cc/(Ff) \times 100 and K = F/C.

Step 1, weight balance:

F = C + T \qquad (1)

Step 2, metal balance (correct sampling, weighing and assaying):

Ff = Cc + Tt \qquad (2)

Step 3. Multiply (1) by t and subtract from (2):

Ft = Ct + Tt \quad\Rightarrow\quad F(f - t) = C(c - t)

Step 4, ratio of concentration:

K = \frac{F}{C} = \frac{c - t}{f - t}

Step 5, recovery. Put C/F = (f - t)/(c - t) into the definition:

\boxed{R = \frac{c\,(f - t)}{f\,(c - t)} \times 100}

Only assays are needed. Example: f = 2.1\%, c = 55.1\%, t = 0.1\% Pb gives K = 27.5 to 1 and R = 95.4\%.
pts: Defines recovery as the percentage of feed metal reporting to the concentrate, R = Cc/Ff \times 100
Defines ratio of concentration as F/C (for example 20 to 1) and notes it is independent of recovery, so both are needed
Weight balance F = C + T
Metal balance Ff = Cc + Tt
Multiplies by t and subtracts to get F(f - t) = C(c - t)
Ratio of concentration (c - t)/(f - t)
Recovery c(f - t)/[f(c - t)] \times 100, boxed
Notes that only assays are needed, or a numerical check

  • Weight-based and assay-based results differ for real test data (91.8% against 95.4% recovery for the slide test) because of sampling and weighing errors.

7b.html:
A particle smaller than the aperture does not pass at once, for two reasons.

1. Probability of hitting the screen matrix. Only part of the screen area is open, so a particle may land on the wire. For a sphere of diameter d on a square aperture D_A with wire D_W:

P = \left(\frac{D_A - d}{D_A + D_W}\right)^2

With D_W = D_A and d = 0.5D_A, P \approx 6\%, so about 36 presentations are needed for a 90% chance; near-mesh particles need far more. Particles must be presented to the screen many times.

2. Blinding. Particles just greater than the aperture wedge in the openings and block them, cutting the open area.

Role of the two movements.

  • Vertical movement lifts particles out of the blocking positions (unblinds the apertures) and loosens the bed so fines work down to the deck.
  • Horizontal movement ensures that, when the particles fall back under gravity, they land at different positions on the screen, and it carries the oversize to discharge so fresh feed reaches the deck.

Vertical motion alone drops a particle back on the same spot; sliding alone leaves blinding particles wedged. The vibrating screen gives both motions and is much more efficient than a static bar screen, on which material only slides down.
pts: Only part of the screen is open: a particle may hit the matrix, so it must be presented many times
Probability of passage, for example P = [(D_A - d)/(D_A + D_W)]^2, falls as d approaches D_A
Near-mesh particles blind the apertures
Vertical movement lifts blinding particles out of the apertures and loosens the bed
Horizontal movement presents the falling particles at different positions and conveys the oversize
Either movement alone fails (same aperture again, or blinding particles stay wedged)
Vibrating screen provides both and is far more efficient than a static bar screen

7c.html:
Classification is a method of separating mineral particles of various sizes, shapes and specific gravities into two or more products on the basis of the velocity with which they fall through a fluid (usually water: wet classifying). Coarse, heavier and rounder grains settle faster than finer, lighter and more angular ones. It is used for particles too fine to be screened efficiently.

Principle.

  1. Terminal velocity. Gravity (less buoyancy) accelerates a particle, while the fluid resistance rises with velocity. When they balance, the particle reaches its terminal velocity and falls uniformly.
  2. Resistance. At low velocity it is viscous (shear); at high velocity turbulent (fluid displacement). In the viscous range Stokes' law applies:
v_t = \frac{d^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)\,g}{18\,\mu}

For equal density the larger particle falls faster; for equal size the denser one does.

  1. Sorting column. Fluid rises at a uniform velocity V: particles with v_t > V sink to the spigot, those with v_t < V go to the overflow.
  2. Size and density together. In water at 20 degrees C (\mu = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{Pa\,s}), 50 μm quartz (2.7) settles at 2.3 mm/s and 50 μm galena (7.5) at 8.9 mm/s, so galena of 50 μm reports with quartz of about 98 μm.
  3. Free and hindered settling. Below about 15% solids, particles settle freely and size dominates (horizontal-current, sedimentation classifiers). In denser pulps crowding makes the pulp act as a heavy liquid; this hindered settling raises the effect of density (vertical-current classifiers).
pts: Defines classification: separation into two or more products by settling velocity in a fluid, which depends on size, specific gravity and shape
Coarse, heavy, round grains settle faster; used for particles too fine to screen
Gravity against resistance rising with velocity; at balance, terminal velocity and uniform fall
Viscous and turbulent resistance; Stokes' law or the rule that larger or denser particles settle faster
Sorting column (described or sketched): fluid rising at V; v_t > V to the spigot, v_t < V to the overflow
Example showing size and density act together (equal-settling 50 μm galena and about 98 μm quartz)
Free settling (below about 15% solids, size dominant) and hindered settling (density effect increased) and the classifier types that use them

• Column with fluid rising at V; overflow (v_t < V, fine, light) at the top, spigot product (v_t > V, coarse, dense) at the bottom.
  • Particle with weight down and buoyancy and drag up.

7c.watch:
• The question has two parts: a one-sentence definition, then the mechanism. The terminal velocity and the sorting column carry most of the "principle" marks.
  • Stokes' law holds only for fine particles (small Reynolds number, below roughly 50 to 100 μm in water); coarser particles pass through an intermediate range into the turbulent (Newton) regime, reached at a few millimetres.

8a.html:
Principle. When a mixture of magnetic and non-magnetic particles is carried across a magnetic field, the magnetic particles tend to stay in the field while the others pass through. The separator simply provides two paths: a gravitational path for the non-magnetic particles and a magnetic path for the magnetic ones.

Construction.

  • A rotating drum whose shell is non-magnetic (for example stainless steel), turning at a set speed.
  • Inside it, a stationary assembly of magnets (permanent or electromagnets) covering an arc of the drum on the feed side, with poles of alternating polarity (N, S, N, ...). As particles pass the alternating poles they turn over, which releases non-magnetic particles trapped among the magnetic ones.
  • A feed hopper or vibrating feeder above the drum, and a splitter below it dividing the tails bin from the magnetics bin.

Functioning.

  1. Dry feed falls in a thin, even layer onto the top of the rotating drum.
  2. As the particles reach the field, those with magnetic susceptibility are attracted toward the magnets but are stopped by the drum surface, so they are held on the shell and carried round with it.
  3. Non-magnetic particles feel no pull; gravity and the centrifugal force throw them off the drum on their normal trajectory into the tails bin.
  4. When the held particles pass the end of the magnet arc, the field vanishes and they drop (or are brushed off) on the far side of the splitter as mags.

Control and use. Field strength, drum speed (faster gives a cleaner but smaller magnetic product), feed rate and splitter position set the cut. Dry drums suit coarse feeds, up to about 120-150 mm; below about 6-8 mm wet separation is often better, because water stops magnetic and non-magnetic particles sticking together.
pts: Neat labelled sketch: feed, rotating drum, stationary magnets inside, tails, mags and splitter
Principle: magnetic particles stay in the field, giving a magnetic path and a gravitational path
Construction: rotating non-magnetic drum around a stationary arc of magnets of alternating polarity
Dry feed delivered in a thin layer onto the top of the drum
Non-magnetic particles leave on their normal (gravity and centrifugal) trajectory into the tails
Magnetic particles are held on the shell, carried past the end of the magnets and released into the mags bin beyond the splitter
Operating variables (field, speed, feed rate, splitter) or the size range for dry separation (coarse, 120-150 mm; wet better below 6-8 mm)

  • Rotating non-magnetic drum with the stationary magnet arc (alternating N and S) inside it.

  • The magnetic product drops on the far side of the drum from the tails; keep the two bins separated by a splitter.

8b.html:
Frothers are heteropolar, surface-active organic reagents added in small amounts (50-300 g/t) to a flotation pulp to produce a stable froth. Examples: pine oil and cresylic acid.

Their molecules adsorb at the air-water interface, polar group in the water and hydrocarbon chain in the air, and lower the surface tension. This stabilises the bubbles so that they carry the hydrophobic mineral to the surface without bursting and hold it in a froth that is skimmed off. The froth must not be too stable to handle. Ideally frothers do not affect the mineral's floatability.
pts: Defines a frother as a surface-active reagent added in small quantity to produce a stable froth
Gives an example (pine oil, cresylic acid)
Adsorbs at the air-water interface and lowers the surface tension
Stabilises the bubbles so the mineral is carried to the surface and skimmed, without changing the mineral's floatability

8c.html:
The process. Air bubbles are passed through a pulp of fine mineral particles in water. Particles that water does not wet (hydrophobic) attach to the bubbles, rise and form a froth on the surface, which is skimmed off as the concentrate. Wetted (hydrophilic) particles stay in the pulp and leave as tailings.

Driving force. Attachment replaces a solid-liquid and a liquid-gas interface by a new solid-gas interface. It is stable only if the surface energy of the system falls. Per unit area:

\Delta G = \gamma_{sg} - (\gamma_{sl} + \gamma_{lg}) < 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \gamma_{sg} - \gamma_{sl} < \gamma_{lg}

With Young's equation at the three-phase contact, \gamma_{sg} = \gamma_{sl} + \gamma_{lg}\cos\theta, where \theta is the contact angle measured through the water:

\Delta G = \gamma_{lg}(\cos\theta - 1)

So a mineral with a larger contact angle attaches more strongly; when \theta \approx 0 the mineral is fully wetted and \Delta G \approx 0.

Why minerals differ. Breaking ionic or covalent bonds leaves charged surface sites that attract polar water molecules, so most minerals are hydrophilic. Solids held by van der Waals forces (sulphur, graphite, talc, molybdenite) leave uncharged surfaces and are naturally hydrophobic. Hence collectors are adsorbed to make the chosen mineral hydrophobic, and a frother keeps the bubbles and froth stable.

Limits. Only fairly fine particles float: if a particle is too large, its weight (and the fluid motion) exceeds the bubble-particle adhesion and the bubble drops its load.

Direct and reverse flotation. Normally the value mineral goes to the froth and the gangue stays in the pulp (direct flotation); in reverse flotation the gangue is floated.
pts: Describes the process: bubbles through a pulp, hydrophobic particles attach and rise into a froth that is skimmed; hydrophilic particles stay in the pulp
Driving force is the reduction of surface energy: a solid-gas interface replaces solid-liquid and liquid-gas, so attachment needs \gamma_{sg} - \gamma_{sl} < \gamma_{lg}
Contact angle with Young's equation, \Delta G = \gamma_{lg}(\cos\theta - 1), larger \theta means more hydrophobic
Links wettability to bonding: broken ionic or covalent bonds give charged, hydrophilic surfaces; van der Waals-bonded solids (the course book adds hydrogen-bonded ones) are hydrophobic
States that collectors impart hydrophobicity to the chosen mineral and a frother stabilises the froth
Only fine particles float, because a large particle's weight exceeds the adhesion to the bubble
Distinguishes direct flotation (mineral floated) from reverse flotation (gangue floated)

8c.watch:
• The contact angle is measured through the liquid; a hydrophobic surface has a large \theta.
  • Being hydrophobic is necessary but not sufficient: fluid motion and particle mass also act against attachment, which is why the size range is limited.
  • The course book quotes flotation of material as fine as a theoretical 2000 mesh; the coarse limit, not the fine one, is the usual exam point.
  • The course book also calls hydrogen-bonded solids hydrophobic; that is doubtful, because a surface with broken hydrogen bonds hydrogen-bonds to water (ice and gypsum wet readily). The naturally floatable minerals are van der Waals solids such as graphite, sulphur, talc and molybdenite.
